title: Talking About Yourself
description: Longer sentences about your life: where you have lived, your family and work, what you like, and your plans. Watch how time words like sudah, pernah, dulu and waktu do the work of English tenses.

items.indonesian: Saya sudah tinggal di sini selama dua tahun.
items.english: I've been living here for two years.
items.pitfallNote: English needs 'have been living'; Indonesian just adds sudah. Selama is 'for' a length of time.

items.indonesian: Saya belum pernah ke Bali.
items.english: I've never been to Bali.
items.registerNotes: Belum pernah (not yet ever) is the usual way to say this, and it leaves the door open. Tidak pernah sounds final, as if you never mean to go.

items.indonesian: Waktu kecil, saya tinggal di Wellington.
items.english: When I was little, I lived in Wellington.
items.registerNotes: Waktu kecil (when small) is the everyday way to say 'as a child'. Waktu sets the time, so tinggal stays as it is.

items.indonesian: Saya guru bahasa Inggris di sekolah dasar.
items.english: I'm an English teacher at a primary school.
items.pitfallNote: No 'am' and no 'a': Saya guru is 'I'm a teacher'. What you teach comes after: guru bahasa Inggris.

items.indonesian: Dulu saya kerja di bank, tapi sekarang saya punya usaha sendiri.
items.english: I used to work in a bank, but now I run my own business.
items.registerNotes: Dulu at the start means 'in the past, used to', and sekarang brings you back to now. Punya usaha sendiri (have your own business) is how people say they're self-employed.

items.indonesian: Saya sudah menikah, tapi belum punya anak.
items.english: I'm married, but we don't have children yet.
items.cultureNote: Marriage and children come up early in conversation. Belum (not yet) is the gentle, usual answer: it doesn't sound final.

items.indonesian: Suami saya orang Indonesia, dari Medan.
items.english: My husband's Indonesian, from Medan.
items.registerNotes: Orang plus a country gives a nationality: orang Indonesia, orang Selandia Baru. Dari plus a city says where in the country.

items.indonesian: Saya anak bungsu dari tiga bersaudara.
items.english: I'm the youngest of three.
items.cultureNote: People often describe themselves by birth order: anak sulung (eldest), anak tengah (middle), anak bungsu (youngest). Expect to be asked where you come.

items.indonesian: Kakak saya tinggal di Australia, tapi orang tua saya masih di Auckland.
items.english: My older brother lives in Australia, but my parents are still in Auckland.
items.pitfallNote: Orang tua (literally 'old people') means parents. Masih is 'still', and there's no 'are': masih di Auckland.

items.indonesian: Biasanya saya bangun jam enam dan langsung mandi.
items.english: I usually get up at six and have a shower straight away.
items.registerNotes: Biasanya at the start sets the frame for everything after it. Langsung is 'straight away'.
items.cultureNote: Many Indonesians mandi twice a day, in the morning and the late afternoon, to stay fresh in the heat.

items.indonesian: Saya sering lupa nama orang.
items.english: I often forget people's names.
items.registerNotes: Sering (often) goes before the verb. A kind way to ask for a name again: Maaf, saya sering lupa nama orang.

items.indonesian: Hobi saya mendaki gunung dan berenang di laut.
items.english: My hobbies are hiking and swimming in the sea.
items.pitfallNote: No 'are' and no '-ing': Hobi saya plus the verbs is the whole sentence.

items.indonesian: Saya tertarik dengan budaya Jawa.
items.english: I'm interested in Javanese culture.
items.pitfallNote: Tertarik takes dengan or pada, not di: tertarik dengan, interested in.

items.indonesian: Aku nggak terlalu suka pedas, sih.
items.english: I'm not really into spicy food, to be honest.
items.registerNotes: Casual, to friends. Sih on the end softens the admission. To someone older: Saya kurang suka pedas.

items.indonesian: Saya belajar bahasa Indonesia supaya bisa mengobrol dengan keluarga pacar saya.
items.english: I'm learning Indonesian so I can chat with my partner's family.
items.pitfallNote: Each owner follows the thing it owns, so read keluarga pacar saya backwards: my partner's family.

items.indonesian: Waktu pertama kali datang ke sini, saya tidak bisa bahasa Indonesia sama sekali.
items.english: When I first came here, I couldn't speak any Indonesian at all.
items.registerNotes: Bisa alone covers 'can speak' a language: Saya bisa bahasa Indonesia. Tidak … sama sekali is 'not … at all'.

items.indonesian: Sejak pindah ke Jakarta, saya jarang masak sendiri.
items.english: Since moving to Jakarta, I hardly ever cook for myself.
items.registerNotes: Jarang (rarely) goes before the verb, like sering. Sendiri after a verb is 'yourself': masak sendiri, cook for yourself.

items.indonesian: Saya pernah mencoba durian, tapi tidak suka baunya.
items.english: I've tried durian, but I didn't like the smell.
items.registerNotes: Pernah says you've done something at some point. Baunya is 'its smell': the -nya stands for the durian.

items.indonesian: Saya baru pulang dari liburan di Lombok.
items.english: I've just got back from a holiday in Lombok.
items.pitfallNote: Baru before a verb is 'just': baru pulang, just got back. After a noun it's 'new': rumah baru.

items.indonesian: Aku kangen banget sama keluargaku.
items.english: I really miss my family.
items.registerNotes: Casual, to a friend. Sama is the spoken 'with' after a feeling, and -ku is 'my'. To someone older: Saya kangen sekali dengan keluarga saya.

items.indonesian: Rencananya saya mau cuti dua minggu bulan depan.
items.english: I'm planning to take two weeks off next month.
items.registerNotes: Rencananya (the plan is) is a handy way into plans that are not fixed yet. Cuti is leave you take from work; libur is a day off for everyone.

items.indonesian: Kalau ada waktu, saya ingin belajar masak makanan Indonesia.
items.english: If I get the time, I'd like to learn to cook Indonesian food.
items.registerNotes: Ingin is a slightly more formal 'would like' than mau, good for wishes and hopes. Kalau ada waktu is literally 'if there's time'.

items.indonesian: Saya agak gugup kalau harus bicara di depan banyak orang.
items.english: I get a bit nervous when I have to speak in front of a lot of people.
items.registerNotes: Kalau here is 'whenever', not 'if'. Agak (a bit) softens a feeling.

items.indonesian: Aku lagi belajar naik motor, tapi masih takut.
items.english: I'm learning to ride a scooter, but I'm still scared.
items.registerNotes: Casual: lagi before a verb is '-ing', the spoken sedang. To someone older: Saya sedang belajar naik motor, tapi masih takut.

items.indonesian: Saya bangga sekali waktu anak saya lulus kuliah.
items.english: I was so proud when my son graduated from university.
items.registerNotes: Waktu (when) puts the whole sentence in the past, so nothing else needs to change. Lulus is to pass or to graduate.
